title: Cape Cod
hook: he walks the shore and faces the sea's indifference (Cape Cod)

segments.voice: Yesterday, contact: Thoreau coming down Ktaadn, crying out at plain rock and wind. What did your hand meet when you touched something on purpose? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

A book about a beach that begins with a shipwreck. Thoreau sets out to walk the outer shore of Cape Cod, and on the way he passes a wreck: a ship broken on the rocks, people from the village searching the sand, wooden boxes laid out for the dead. It is a hard way to open a book about the seaside. He doesn't dress it up, and he doesn't look away. And what stays with him afterward isn't only the bodies and the boxes. It's the sea itself, which goes on breaking against the shore as if nothing had happened.
screen: `A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH A WRECK.` → `HE DOESN'T LOOK AWAY.` → `THE SEA GOES ON.`

segments.voice: First, the wreck. Thoreau describes the searching and the boxes plainly, with care for the people standing there. Then he notices the waves. The same sea that broke the ship goes on rolling in. He doesn't pretend it mourns. Second, no flattery. Later he calls the seashore a wild, rank place, and says "there is no flattery in it." A garden is arranged for us. A view from a porch seems to be laid out for our pleasure. The outer beach is not. Crabs, weed, wreckage, whatever the water throws up. It isn't against us. It simply isn't about us. Third, neutral ground. He describes the shore as a kind of neutral ground, between land and sea, belonging fully to neither. A place where you can't quite pretend the world was built around you. Fourth, the last line of the book. After all that walking, he stands at the edge and writes, "A man may stand there and put all America behind him." Every argument, every town, every errand, at his back. In front: only water that doesn't know his name. Some readers find that bleak. Others find it a relief. The sea's indifference can be a kind of freedom: nothing to perform, nobody to impress. This week we've followed Thoreau from a jail cell to a wild mountainside, from conscience to contact. Here at the shore, the whole country is behind him, and the sea doesn't care who he is.
screen: `THE WRECK, AND THE SEA GOING ON.` · `THERE IS NO FLATTERY IN IT.` · `A NEUTRAL GROUND.` · then, large: `ALL AMERICA BEHIND HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face something big. If you can, stand at a window or step outside and look at the widest view you've got: a skyline, a field, a parking lot, the sky. If you can't, close your eyes and bring to mind a sea or a plain you've seen. Let it be bigger than you. Notice that it isn't watching you, isn't grading you, isn't waiting for you to say anything. Let your shoulders drop a little at that. Put one thing that's been nagging you behind you, the way Thoreau put the country at his back. The bell holds the time.
Cape Cod. Thoreau's book of walking the outer shore, which opens with a wreck and ends with the whole country at his back. Today's word.
Your line: the indifferent sea. Today, when something feels like it's all about you, find a sky, a tree or a long view, and let it not care for a moment. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Some readers of Thoreau's Cape Cod notice how plainly he looks at the sea, which is neither cruel nor kind; some go to a shore or a wide view to feel how small their own worries look beside it.

fork.setup: you're Thoreau, on a shore where a ship has just been wrecked. the sea keeps rolling in. what do you write?
options: that the sea is cruel and wicked.
that the sea mourns with the town.
that the sea goes on, neither kind nor cruel.
fork.reveal: he doesn't make the sea a villain or a mourner. it simply goes on. the indifference is the point.
